Creator Partnerships Outside Crypto Make the Same Mistakes With Fewer Excuses.

Analysislowob research

By lowob · 22 July 2026 · 7-minute read · Growth

Web3 spent several years and a great deal of money learning what creator partnerships do and do not do: reach that produced nothing, screenshots instead of evidence, undisclosed payments, and audiences that turned out to be other creators. Fintech and AI companies now moving budget into the same channel can read those lessons, and regulators have turned several of them into rules. The FTC's 2024 rule bans buying fake followers and views, its Endorsement Guides make advertisers liable for deceptive endorsements, and the FCA holds firms responsible for financial promotions their influencers make. Creators are worth doing well, as a programme rather than a set of posts.

Why the channel is worth doing well

For a category the ad platforms restrict, creators are one of the few channels where the product can be explained, at length, by someone the audience already trusts. A personal-finance creator can walk through a new account product in eight minutes. An AI tooling creator can show a workflow from start to finish. No paid placement offers that.

The money is moving. The Performance Marketing Association's 2025 industry study, conducted with London Research, put US affiliate and performance partnership investment at about $13.6 billion in 2024. Financial services rose from 12% to 15% of that spend, and content creators and bloggers took a larger share of investment. This is trade-body research, but the direction is consistent with what fintech teams report.

The channel is also thinly bid relative to its value, for the unglamorous reason that it takes work. Recruiting, briefing, tracking and paying two hundred creators is a programme, not a media buy. Most companies will not build it, which is why the price is still reasonable.

The five mistakes, translated

Buying reach instead of audience. A creator with a million followers who are mostly other creators, or mostly outside the geography the product serves, produces impressions and nothing else. Ask for audience composition, geography and evidence of past products the audience adopted, then run one small test before believing any of it. Our guide to reading a creator media kit covers what to request. Fake reach is now also a legal problem: the FTC's rule on consumer reviews and testimonials, in force since 21 October 2024, prohibits buying or selling fake indicators of social media influence, such as followers, views and likes generated by bots, where the buyer knew or should have known they were fake.

Briefing a script instead of a job. A creator handed approved claims and asked for enthusiasm produces an ad, and the audience knows. A creator briefed on the real problem, the product truth, what may not be said and the question the audience will ask produces an explanation in their own words. The second converts. The first gets skipped.

Paying flat when the product converts. A creator paid a flat fee is paid for publishing. A creator paid per activated account, approved application or retained subscriber is paid for the outcome, and will tell you quickly whether the product converts with their audience. For products that do convert, cost-per-outcome terms are cheaper and self-correcting. For products that do not convert yet, creators are the wrong channel, and the flat fee only hides that.

Treating disclosure as a formality. The FTC's Endorsement Guides, revised in June 2023, require material connections such as payment, free product and affiliate commissions to be disclosed clearly and conspicuously. The revision says a disclosure must be "unavoidable", so one hidden behind a "more" link does not count, and that advertisers are liable for deceptive endorsements and must run "reasonable programs" to train and monitor endorsers. The FTC's influencer guidance adds that video disclosures belong in the video, not only the description, and that a creator cannot describe experience with a product they have not tried. AI companies should note that the 2023 revision says virtual, AI-generated influencers can count as endorsers.

Measuring at the post. Views and engagement describe the post. Accounts, applications, activations and retention describe the business. Give every creator a link, code or landing page the company controls, and report on outcomes the company's own tracking confirmed. KOL campaigns need more than impression screenshots covers the reporting standard.

MistakeFixRule or evidence behind it
Buying reachAudience data plus one paid testFTC rule bans buying fake followers and views
Scripted briefBrief the job, the limits and the likely questionAudience trust depends on the creator's own words
Flat feePay per verified outcome once the product convertsOutcome pay exposes poor fit within weeks
Disclosure as formalitySpecify wording in the brief; check every postFTC guides: disclosure must be unavoidable; advertisers liable
Post-level reportingCompany-controlled links and codes, outcome reportsOnly confirmed outcomes connect to revenue

Financial products carry an extra layer

For financial products, disclosure is the floor, not the ceiling. What the creator may claim is regulated too.

The UK is the clearest case. The FCA's FG24/1 guidance says firms working with affiliate marketers such as influencers "should take proactive responsibility" for them, and should consider how to monitor their partners' marketing. An influencer who promotes a regulated product without approval from an authorised person may be committing a criminal offence under section 21 of FSMA, punishable by up to two years' imprisonment. Each promotion must be standalone compliant, and firms should not rely on the social platform to keep their records.

The FCA enforces this. In a week of action starting 20 April 2026, as one of 17 regulators taking part, it made 120 account takedown requests, issued 34 warning alerts and identified 1,267 illegal financial adverts on Meta platforms reaching at least 2.3 million UK accounts.

A regulator does not distinguish between the creator's mistake and the company's. Neither should your programme.

In the US, the FTC's endorsement rules apply across consumer categories, and other regulators add their own for specific products. The SEC's marketing rule, for example, requires an investment adviser's advertisements to disclose clearly and prominently whether a promoter is a client and whether they are paid. The brief should carry the approved claims and disclosure language, and the programme should check compliance before and after posting, because the FTC's guidance notes it is easier to review posts before they go live than to search for them afterwards.

Choosing the tier

Creators are not one channel. They are three, with different jobs.

TierJobHow to payHow to measure
A handful of authoritiesChange what an audience believes; launches and products that need explainingNegotiated fee, sometimes with an outcome elementComprehension and qualified action, not volume
A middle tier of subject-matter creatorsThe core of a performance programmeCost per outcome, structured briefs, monthly creative refreshVerified outcomes and cost per outcome
A long tail of small creatorsVolume at the best unit costPublic terms, paid per outcome, run as a channelCost per outcome; accept unpredictable volume

The long tail often produces the best cost per outcome and the least predictable volume. A programme needs all three tiers, in proportions that match the product's stage. A company that buys only the first tier has a launch. A company that builds only the third has a channel with no story.

The structure that makes it a channel

Written terms. A standard brief. Product access and an FAQ. Creative the creator can adapt. Tracking per creator. A named person who answers within a day. A monthly review of who is producing outcomes and who is producing posts. Clear disclosure language and a compliance check.

That is a programme. It is the same programme Web3 needed and mostly did not build. Our Partner channel design covers how to set roles and pay across partner types, and Referral partners without leakage covers registering and paying for introductions so the economics hold. The companies entering the channel from fintech and AI have no excuse for skipping it, and every reason to build it before their competitors clear the review queue.

lowob takeaways

  • Buy audience, not reach. Ask for composition and past adoption, test small, and treat bought followers as a legal risk as well as a waste.
  • Brief the job, not the script. The creator's own explanation converts; approved claims and limits keep it safe.
  • Pay per outcome once the product converts. A flat fee pays for publishing and hides poor fit.
  • Own disclosure and compliance. The advertiser is liable in the US and responsible in the UK; specify the wording and check every post.
  • Run the long tail as a channel. Public terms, pay per outcome and a monthly review turn small creators into the best unit cost.

Common questions

Do fintech companies need to disclose paid influencer partnerships?

Yes. In the US, the FTC requires material connections such as payment, free product or affiliate commissions to be disclosed clearly and unavoidably, and holds advertisers liable for deceptive endorsements. In the UK, firms are responsible for financial promotions their influencers make.

Can an influencer promote a financial product in the UK?

Only if the promotion is made or approved by an FCA-authorised person and meets the financial promotion rules. The FCA says unauthorised influencers promoting regulated products without approval may be committing a criminal offence.

Should you pay creators a flat fee or per result?

Pay per verified outcome, such as an activated account or approved application, once the product converts. Flat fees pay for publishing and hide whether the audience adopts the product.

Is it illegal to buy followers for an influencer campaign?

In the US, the FTC's rule in force since October 2024 prohibits buying or selling fake indicators of social media influence, such as bot followers and views, for commercial purposes where the buyer knew or should have known they were fake.

Next move

Take your current creator brief and check it for three things: the approved claims and the claims that may not be made, the exact disclosure wording, and the outcome you will pay for. If any is missing, rewrite the brief before the next creator posts.
